1	# live-spec
     2	
     3	**Ten working [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) skills, plus the one shared rulebook they all load. They turn a wish spoken in passing into a specified, reviewed, tested, committed change. Scripts block the push when the documents and the code disagree.**
     4	
     5	---
     6	
     7	You tell your agent *"the report page needs a date filter"* and four minutes later it is written, tested, and green. The tests pass because they came from the same spec. The spec never said what happens when the date is invalid, so the agent picked some behaviour and shipped it. Nobody chose that behaviour and nobody reviewed it, and the green suite never looked at it.
     8	
     9	That is the gap. The spec became the thing your agent builds from, and nothing checks the spec itself.
    10	
    11	live-spec closes it. You say the sentence in passing, with nothing to file and no form. It gets classified, written into a living spec, reviewed by a formal-verification pass, covered by tests derived from that spec, coded until green, and committed with its documents in one change. A script on the pre-push hook compares the spec to the code that shipped and refuses the push when the two disagree. There is no CLI. You talk to it.
    12	
    13	---
    14	
    15	## Install
    16	
    17	There are two ways in. Pick one road at step 1, then follow that road's lines wherever the steps below fork.
    18	
    19	### Step 1 — get the pack onto your machine
    20	
    21	**The plugin road.** Type two lines into Claude Code:
    22	
    23	```
    24	/plugin marketplace add happysasha18/live-spec
    25	/plugin install live-spec@live-spec
    26	```
    27	
    28	That is the whole step. The plugin puts the entire pack tree under `~/.claude/plugins/cache/`. You do not clone this repository, now or later.
    29	
    30	**The clone road.** Clone the repository and run its installer:
    31	
    32	```
    33	git clone https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec.git
    34	cd live-spec && ./install.sh
    35	```
    36	
    37	`install.sh` copies the skill folders into `~/.claude/skills/` and copies nothing else. Keep the clone. It is your copy of the pack tree, and step 3 runs a script that lives inside it.
    38	
    39	### Step 2 — attach the pack to a project
    40	
    41	Both roads do the same thing here. Open the project in Claude Code and say *"attach live-spec to this project"*, or *"found a new project on live-spec"* in an empty directory. The pack locates its own tree and reads yours, then runs the setup walk that fits. [`adopt/START.md`](adopt/START.md) founds a fresh project; [`adopt/ADOPT.md`](adopt/ADOPT.md) attaches an existing codebase and writes your first spec from what your code ships today. [`docs/adoption.md`](docs/adoption.md) tells the same story in plainer words.
    42	
    43	### Step 3 — install the push gate
    44	
    45	The push gate is a separate step, and it reads the documents step 2 just wrote. **The setup walk offers to install it for you.** That is the ordinary path. Read on only if you would rather do it by hand.
    46	
    47	By hand, run one script from your project's root. It lives in the pack tree you already got in step 1, so the line you type depends on which road you took:
    48	
    49	```
    50	# plugin road — the tree sits in the plugin cache
    51	bash ~/.claude/plugins/cache/*/live-spec/*/adopt/install-scaffold.sh
    52	
    53	# clone road — the tree is the clone from step 1
    54	bash /path/to/live-spec/adopt/install-scaffold.sh
    55	```
    56	
    57	It copies the four checks into your project's `guardrails/` and seeds `guardrails.config.json`.
    58	
    59	That config then needs two things from you. Fill in your paths: the spec, the test matrix, the queue, the tests, and the surface registry. The queue is the dated list of what has been asked of the product and where each ask stands. This repository keeps its own in [`ROADMAP.md`](ROADMAP.md).
    60	
    61	Second, empty the config's `waivers` block. It ships holding one example waiver, and that example switches the completeness check off. Leave the example in place and you run on three checks instead of four, with nothing to tell you.
    62	
    63	Last, add the four check lines to `.git/hooks/pre-push`. They are listed in [`scaffold/guardrails/README.md`](scaffold/guardrails/README.md). Create that hook file if your project has none, and make it executable. The checks run on your next push.
    64	
    65	The checks need Python 3.9 or newer, and a project that is already a git repository.
    66	
    67	After that everything runs in plain words: any wish, *"status"*, *"publish"*.
    68	
    69	---
    70	
    71	## What the spec looks like
    72	
    73	A project under the pack keeps one document, `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, stating what the product promises today. A stranger can read a section on the first pass. The format is a requirements genre, defined in [`docs/spec-format.md`](docs/spec-format.md):
    74	
    75	- The document opens with a **glossary**. Every domain noun used anywhere in the spec has a one-sentence definition. An ordinary English word needs no entry.

    10	The document opens with a glossary that defines every domain noun, then a body of
    11	requirements: each carries a short context (when the situation arises, who is involved, what the

    13	`[E-6, T-12]` trail at line ends as anchors for the machine; a reader can ignore them. A generated code-to-location table
    14	closes the document. The pack's own spec is the reference shape; its version lives in `VERSION`.
    15	
    16	The spec is living in a precise sense. Work enters it before code: a new behaviour arrives as a spec
    17	delta, gets reviewed, and only then gets built. Shipped behaviour traces back to it: a guardrail
    18	check goes red when a user-facing behaviour has no spec sentence behind it. And it stays current:
    19	a removed feature leaves a dated tombstone, and history moves to `JOURNAL.md`.
    20	
    21	## The pipeline — a wish becomes shipped, tested work
    22	
    23	A wish is a request in plain words, thrown at any moment. It becomes one row in the queue,
    24	`ROADMAP.md`, the moment it is spoken (SPEC E-2). Intake names its door aloud — feature,
    25	bug, refactor, docs-only, skip — before any code; fixed tripwires decide, so a casual ask that
    26	creates a new surface still enters as a feature (SPEC T-12). A feature walks nine stations in order.
    27	
    28	1. **Spec** — `spec-author` writes the delta: entities, states, transitions, invariants, regression
    29	   fences on touched live surfaces, a sweep of the standard facets (the viewport bands, touch,
    30	   the empty and error states, keyboard reach), non-goals, one success measure.
    31	2. **Prove** — `product-prover` reviews the grown spec; findings are recorded and folded.
    32	3. **Architecture** — `ARCHITECTURE.md` maps named nodes, each owning spec facts, pinned to real
    33	   `file:line`. The document also owes a runtime view (each promised flow walked node by node, with
    34	   a fallback at every failure point, INV-74) and a placement view saying where every node runs (INV-75).
    35	4. **Prove the architecture** — the prover again, with an architecture lens: every fact owned,
    36	   every node backed by the spec, every seam named, both views present.
    37	5. **Test matrix** — `test-author` derives `TEST_MATRIX.md`, one block per node, one row per fact;
    38	   every row states what the fact does and what it must never do, and pins a test level (string /
    39	   DOM-text / browser-computed / pixel).
    40	6. **Tests** — written against the real shipped artifact; each new test is watched failing first.
    41	7. **Code** — implement until green; mechanical work goes to cheaper worker models under precise
    42	   briefs, and judgment stays with the senior model.
    43	8. **Verify by deed** — run the real thing and look at it; green means zero failures and exactly
    44	   the expected skip list.
    45	9. **Commit and show** — docs travel with the change; the human sees the real render; accepted
    46	   work is pushed to the host's remote by rule, the README re-checked at every push (INV-82).
    47	
    48	A bug shortcuts to matrix → test → code. A refactor changes no behaviour, so it enters at the verify
    49	station with the full suite and an audit of the touched matrix sections. A docs-only change re-reads the
    50	changed section as it renders, plus one search for a claim the code no longer supports. The skip door
    51	covers a one-file edit that adds no state and no visible behaviour, and it still ships a test.
    52

    54	empty surface, a behaviour without a spec sentence, or a duplicated anchor turns the push red. The
    55	host wires that hook itself, in the second install step the README states. The normative walk lives
    56	in `skills/build-pipeline/SKILL.md`.
    57	
    58	## The prover is a formal-review step
    59	
    60	`product-prover` reads documents the way a formal-methods reviewer reads a model: entities, states,
    61	transitions, invariants, safety, liveness, atomicity, and the composition between surfaces. It runs
    62	at two stations (spec and architecture) and, on the pack itself, again before every push. Findings
    63	land in dated files under `docs/prover/`. Each one carries a marked fate with a reason — folded,
    64	queued, recorded, rejected, or still open — so the fate of every defect stays checkable after a
    65	memory wipe. The prover finds holes in what documents
    66	claim; the tests then cover the facts.
    67	
    68	## The settings ladder
    69	
    70	How the pack behaves is a named setting living in one of four nested scopes; a narrower scope wins.
    71	The normative table and the default values live in `skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md` (SPEC E-13).
    72	
    73	| Scope | Home | Describes |
    74	|---|---|---|
    75	| package defaults | `live-spec-base` | the pack out of the box |
    76	| personal profile | `~/.claude/live-spec/profile.md` | one human, across all their projects |
    77	| host profile | `<host>/.live-spec/profile.md` | one project |
    78	| session | the human's spoken word | this conversation only |
    79	
    80	An override exists only as a written line in its profile file. Setting one leaves a dated journal
    81	note, so every divergence stays visible. The session scope is spoken only and dies with the conversation; making
    82	it permanent is a promotion into a profile, on the human's word.
    83	
    84	## Ten working skills, plus the one shared rulebook they all load
    85	
    86	- **live-spec-base** — the shared rulebook and the default settings, stated once; on any apparent
    87	  rule conflict, this file wins.
    88	- **spec-author** — writes and grows the living spec, use-case-first and prover-ready.
    89	- **product-prover** — reviews specs and architecture documents with formal-verification thinking.
    90	- **product-prover-pack** — the pack adapter for the external canonical product-prover: the pin
    91	  map, the pack paths, the record home, and the mode names; it reviews nothing itself.
    92	- **design-reviewer** — reviews the design itself once the spec is proven: groups the same-kind
    93	  things the text never declared, checks each kind behaves alike, and brings the strongest likely
    94	  difference to the human. It recommends and questions, leaving the landing free.
    95	- **build-pipeline** — sequences the whole arc from wish to shipped, tested, committed change.
    96	- **test-author** — derives the matrix from the proven spec and writes the tests.
    97	- **communicator** — shows work plainly and asks only the decisions the human can actually make.
    98	- **feedback-intake** — receives everything a person hands back and routes each item to its home.
    99	- **feedback-collector** — on a rare strong reaction, offers (with your yes) a private note up to the pack's authors; off by default, never sends on its own.
   100	- **text-audit** — reads any human-facing text as a stranger and fixes where a reader stops. It
   101	  closes after two rounds in a row where both fresh readers find nothing blocking.
   102	- **publish** — the quality gate when work leaves the machine, owing what the artifact's kind owes.
   103

   105

   107	and placement views above (INV-74, INV-75). A background worker outlives a memory wipe, so a
   108	resuming session proves it dead or alive before touching shared files (INV-76). The test layer
   109	gained a set of lessons: behaviour past a headless browser's reach gets a real-device walk row; a
   110	geometry fact asserts relative distances, at several viewport sizes, over repeated steps; an engine
   111	extracted from one project tests on its own generic fixtures; and the suite's own plumbing is itself
   112	tested, so a skip path or a wrapper's exit code can never fake a pass (INV-77–INV-80). Every

1	# Adopting the pack in an existing project
     2	
     3	live-spec attaches to a codebase that already has code, documents, and habits. The project that
     4	adopts it is called the **host**. The normative procedure is [adopt/ADOPT.md](../adopt/ADOPT.md);
     5	this page gives the shape of the run, what the host gains, and where the supporting files live.
     6	When this page and ADOPT.md differ, ADOPT.md wins. A project with nothing in it yet takes a
     7	different walk, the founding at [adopt/START.md](../adopt/START.md). Two spoken sentences reach the right one of the
     8	two: "attach live-spec to this project" and "found a new project on live-spec". The routing card the
     9	build-pipeline skill carries is what picks.
    10	
    11	One boundary holds through the whole run: from a host session, the live-spec package repo is
    12	read-only. A defect found during adoption goes into live-spec's `inbox/` as one new file and into
    13	the host's own journal (SPEC INV-10).
    14	
    15	## The procedure at a glance
    16	
    17	ADOPT.md runs as ordered phases; each phase states its own done-condition. In plain terms:
    18	
    19	1. **Version control first (Phase 0).** The host becomes a git repo with a `.gitignore`, one
    20	   baseline commit of the pristine tree, and a recorded decision about a remote. From this point
    21	   the whole run is reversible.
    22	2. **Cruft sweep, offered once (Phase 0.5).** Writing the `.gitignore` surfaces regenerable junk
    23	   such as caches and stale exports. The run lists it in groups and deletes only what the human
    24	   approves.
    25	3. **Orient (Phase 1).** The run loads the human's personal profile, asks the founding questions
    26	   (personal or reusable, what kind of project this is, budget pressure), proposes matching
    27	   skills, and reads every existing document before writing anything. The result is a per-document
    28	   digest under `.live-spec/adopt/`, the run's audit trail.
    29	4. **Inventory (Phase 2).** Every user-facing output, surface, and data entity gets one line with
    30	   a real `file:line` pin. The surfaces seed the surface registry.
    31	5. **Re-engineer existing documents (Phase 3).** What exists turns into the canonical document
    32	   set, keeping the original claims and marking their provenance. Each live surface that lacks
    33	   spec backing gets a human verdict: promote, quarantine, or attic.
    34	6. **Attic over deletion (Phase 4).** Superseded files move to `attic/` with a manifest line,
    35	   via `git mv`, after the human approves the set. Adoption never deletes a host file (INV-7).
    36	7. **Architecture, then tests (Phase 5).** `ARCHITECTURE.md` grows from the inventory's pins;
    37	   `TEST_MATRIX.md` is derived through it, one row per fact under its owning node, each row with
    38	   a test level.
    39	8. **Attach record (Phase 6).** The run records the installed skill versions in `.live-spec/`,
    40	   seeds the host profile, writes its journal entry, and the host joins the standard pipeline.
    41	
    42	The recommended first action after adoption is a full product-prover pass over the spec; ADOPT.md
    43	Phase 6 states the one condition that lets a host skip it.
    44	
    45	## What the host gains
    46	
    47	The canonical document set lives in `adopt/ADOPT.md` — one normative list; the lines below say what
    48	each document does for the host.
    49	
    50	- **A living spec** — `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, use-case-first, with entities, states, transitions,
    51	  invariants, and cross-section composition underneath.
    52	- **An architecture doc and a test matrix** — `ARCHITECTURE.md` names the nodes and seams;
    53	  `TEST_MATRIX.md` derives one pinned-level row per spec fact through them.
    54	- **A journal** — `JOURNAL.md`, dated entries with the why, so history survives memory wipes.
    55	- **A resume file** — `NEXT_STEPS.md`, the one place a cold session reads to continue the work.
    56	- **A queue** — `ROADMAP.md`, where existing TODO items land as rows.
    57	- **A surface registry** — `SURFACE_REGISTRY.md` (or an equivalent gate test), so an unregistered
    58	  rendered surface goes red.
    59	- **Profiles** — the host profile at `.live-spec/profile.md` holds this project's overrides; the
    60	  personal profile at `~/.claude/live-spec/profile.md` holds the human's standing preferences.
    61	  The host file narrows the personal one per the settings ladder (SPEC E-13).
    62	
    63	## Migrating an existing codebase
    64	
    65	Phase 3 of ADOPT.md owns the mapping of existing documents: an existing spec becomes
    66	`PRODUCT_SPEC.md` sections, existing tests become matrix rows cited at their real level, and an
    67	existing roadmap becomes queue rows. Every re-engineered claim starts unverified and gets
    68	reconciled against real code at the first landing that touches its surface. A host whose docs are
    69	already in live-spec shape keeps them as they are; adoption then only fills what is missing,
    70	usually the surface registry and the matrix.
    71	
    72	The mapping is type-aware. The project kind recorded at orient (book, backend service, static
    73	site, fullstack app, CLI, skill pack) sets the spec's primary unit: a feature for an app, a
    74	command or endpoint for a CLI or API, a chapter for a book, a promised guarantee for a
    75	methodology package. The decided format lives in
    76	[docs/spec-format-by-project-type.md](spec-format-by-project-type.md).
    77	
    78	[MIGRATION.md](../MIGRATION.md) covers the other entry: an already-adopted host catching up with
    79	a newer pack. That guide owns the catch-up walk — orient on the delta, one plan behind the
    80	owner's gate, execution that preserves facts, then verify and re-record — and holds the dated
    81	per-version migration chapters the walk applies, oldest first. Each host's own session executes
    82	the walk; nothing outside a host's session writes that host's repo.
    83	
    84	## The scaffold and templates
    85	
    86	`templates/` holds fourteen starter files. Six are the canonical document set:
    87	`PRODUCT_SPEC.template.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.template.md`, `TEST_MATRIX.template.md`,
    88	`ROADMAP.template.md`, `JOURNAL.template.md`, and `NEXT_STEPS.template.md`. Three land on the
    89	project's own word: `DECISIONS.template.md`, `PROBLEMS.template.md`, and `KILL_LIST.template.md`.
    90	The remaining five each carry their own job. `test_scaffold.template.py` is the first runnable
    91	suite, and `agent.template.md` is the tree's agent card. `profile.template.md` is the shape of a
    92	person's own profile, and `skill-review.template.md` the shape of a skill-review record.
    93	`headless_harness.py` is the shared harness for browser-level tests.
    94	
    95	A fresh project gets these through the founding walk, [adopt/START.md](../adopt/START.md). That
    96	walk lands each one under its canonical name, and it stops by name where the pack tree lacks one.
    97	`install.sh` installs the skills alone and reaches no template. An adopted host uses them only for
    98	the documents it lacks, since Phase 3 re-engineers the rest.
    99	The test scaffold lands in `tests/` and defines the minimal green for the first landing.
   100	
   101	`scaffold/guardrails/README.md` is the authoritative description of the four mechanical checks a
   102	host instantiates for its own surfaces: completeness (every rendered surface is registered and
   103	non-empty), tests-present (a diff touching a user-facing module also touches `tests/`),
   104	behaviour-traces-to-spec (every user-facing behaviour names its spec clause), and conflicts
   105	(duplicate IDs, dead references, unmatrixed invariants). Runnable generic check code is a planned
   106	next movement; today each project wires its own instance. `install.sh` at the package root copies
   107	the pack's skills into `~/.claude/skills/`, backing up any existing skill with a timestamp.
   108	
   109	## What stays optional
   110	
   111	- **The remote.** A GitHub remote either exists by the first landing or the human explicitly
   112	  declines one; both outcomes are recorded.
   113	- **The cruft sweep.** The run may skip offering it; deletion without an approval is the only
   114	  forbidden path.
   115	- **The personal profile.** The human may decline creating one; the session then runs on package
